DIGITAL REPLICA PROVISIONS IN PERSONAL AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICES CONTRACTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Studios LLC

WHAT THIS DOCUMENT COVERS: A CONTRACT-FORMATION RULE FOR LIVING PERFORMERS, NOT THE POSTMORTEM DIGITAL-REPLICA LIABILITY STATUTE
California Labor Code section 927, added effective January 1, 2025, addresses a narrow and specific question: whether a particular provision inside a personal-or-professional-services contract — the provision that lets one side create and use a "digital replica" of a living individual's voice or likeness instead of having that individual actually perform the work in person — is enforceable. It regulates contract formation between Taylor Morgan and Acme Studios LLC, not use of an already-existing recording or image after the fact. This is a different statute from this corpus's separate Right of Publicity Demand Letter Information Sheet, which addresses Civil Code section 3344 (a living person's right against unauthorized use of identity) and Civil Code section 3344.1 (a deceased personality's postmortem digital-replica liability, added by a different 2024 bill). Section 927 does not create a liability claim for an unauthorized digital replica the way section 3344.1 does; instead, it makes certain digital-replica contract provisions unenforceable when specific statutory conditions are met, leaving the rest of the contract, and any other legal claim Taylor Morgan might have, untouched.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A provision in an agreement between an individual and any other person for the performance of personal or professional services is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual if the provision meets all of the following conditions:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927 (California Legislative Information text, added by Stats. 2024, ch. 259 (AB 2602), operative Jan. 1, 2025), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions in personal or professional services contracts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what Labor Code section 927 itself covers and how its subject matter (contract-provision enforceability for a living performer's own future contract) differs from Civil Code section 3344.1 (postmortem tort liability for an already-made unauthorized digital replica), both already covered independently elsewhere in this corpus — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific contract provision described using this document falls on one side or the other of that line, which depends on facts this document does not resolve. Labor Code section 927 was added by Stats. 2024, ch. 259 (AB 2602), operative January 1, 2025; it is a brand-new provision, and this document does not represent that any court has yet interpreted it. A CourtListener case-law search for this statute and for "digital replica" California performer contracts was run twice with different search terms and returned, respectively, one unrelated case (a patent/trade-dress dispute with no connection to this statute) and zero results — not a rate-limit failure, but a genuine absence of any case law located, consistent with the statute's newness. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific contract provision is unenforceable under section 927, and completing it does not resolve that question for the individual's or the other contracting party's specific contract.

THE OPERATIVE RULE: UNENFORCEABLE ONLY AS TO A NEW PERFORMANCE FIXED ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2025, AND ONLY IF ALL CONDITIONS ARE MET
Section 927(a)'s own text draws a narrow, conjunctive rule. First, it is limited in time: the provision is unenforceable "only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual." A digital replica of a performance already fixed before that date is not reached by this statute's unenforceability rule at all, on the statute's own terms. Second, the provision is unenforceable only "if the provision meets all of the following conditions" — meaning the statute lists a set of conditions that must all be satisfied together before the digital-replica provision becomes unenforceable, not a list of independent, alternative grounds. Those conditions — described in the following clauses of this document — cover what the provision must lack (a sufficiently specific use description) and how the individual was, or was not, represented when the contract was made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual if the provision meets all of the following conditions"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — temporal scope and all-conditions structure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(a)'s own temporal scope and its all-conditions structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how a court would resolve a dispute over whether a particular performance was "fixed" before or after January 1, 2025, which is a factual and technical question (for example, involving partial recording sessions spanning that date) this document does not address. This clause quotes the same lead-in sentence of subdivision (a) quoted in the companion scope-and-distinction clause of this document; it is not an independent source, only the same sentence read for its temporal-scope and all-conditions structure rather than its overall subject matter. No case law construing the "fixed" requirement or the January 1, 2025 date has been located, for the CourtListener search reasons disclosed in the companion scope clause.

CONDITION ONE: THE PROVISION SUBSTITUTES A DIGITAL REPLICA FOR WORK THE INDIVIDUAL WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE PERFORMED IN PERSON
The first of the statute's listed conditions describes the kind of provision section 927 reaches at all: one that "allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person." On its own terms, this condition targets substitution — a contract clause letting the other contracting party use a digital replica instead of having Taylor Morgan actually show up and perform the work — rather than every contract clause that happens to mention a digital replica for any purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The provision allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual’s voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the in-place-of-in-person-work condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the first listed condition's own wording — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific provision in a particular individual's contract with a particular other party does or does not "allow for the creation and use of a digital replica... in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person," which depends on the specific contract language and is not evaluated here. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(a)(1); the remaining conditions in section 927(a)(2) and (a)(3) are addressed in separate clauses of this document and are not repeated here. No case law construing this condition's "in place of" substitution language has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

CONDITION TWO: A MISSING 'REASONABLY SPECIFIC DESCRIPTION' OF INTENDED USES — UNLESS THE USES MATCH THE CONTRACT'S OWN TERMS AND CHARACTER
The statute's second listed condition looks at what the provision does not say. Under subparagraph (A), except as provided in subparagraph (B), a digital-replica provision satisfies this condition — moving it a step closer to unenforceability — if "the provision does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica." Subparagraph (B) then supplies its own exception: a missing reasonably-specific-use description does not, by itself, make the provision unenforceable if the actual uses made of the digital replica "are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed." Read together, the statute rewards a contract that either specifically describes the digital replica's intended uses up front, or whose actual digital-replica uses stay consistent with the underlying contract's own terms and the fundamental character of what was actually recorded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subparagraph (B), the provision does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the reasonably-specific-description condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  "Failure to include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of a digital replica does not render the provision unenforceable if the uses are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the consistent-uses exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the wording of subparagraphs (A) and (B) of section 927(a)(2) — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific contract provision, or any specific actual use, does or does not satisfy either subparagraph, which depends on facts this document does not evaluate. The quoted text of subparagraph (A) is drawn from leginfo's raw HTML source, which line-wraps mid-sentence (a literal newline-and-tab sequence appears in the source between "reasonably" and "specific description") as a page-formatting artifact of leginfo's own markup, not a gap in the statutory text itself; that whitespace has been normalized to a single space here, and this was verified against leginfo's raw HTML directly rather than assumed. No case law construing either subparagraph, including what counts as "reasonably specific" or what "fundamental character... as recorded or performed" means in a specific dispute, has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

CONDITION THREE: TWO STATUTORY SAFE HARBORS — INDEPENDENT LEGAL COUNSEL, OR A UNION CONTRACT THAT EXPRESSLY ADDRESSES DIGITAL REPLICAS
The statute's third listed condition asks how the individual was represented — or not — when the digital-replica provision was agreed to: "The individual was not represented in any of the following manners." Two manners of representation are listed, and either one takes a provision outside this condition (and so outside the overall unenforceability rule, since all conditions must be met). The first is representation "by legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual's digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual." The second is representation "by a labor union representing workers who do the proposed work, and the terms of their collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses uses of digital replicas."

  "By legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual’s digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the legal-counsel safe harbor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  "By a labor union representing workers who do the proposed work, and the terms of their collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses uses of digital replicas."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the labor-union safe harbor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two representation safe harbors' own wording — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific individual was or was not represented by legal counsel in the manner described, or was or was not covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, when a specific contract was signed, which depends on facts this document does not evaluate. The quoted legal-counsel safe harbor is drawn from leginfo's raw HTML source, which line-wraps mid-sentence (a literal newline-and-tab sequence between "contract" and "or other writing") as a page-formatting artifact of leginfo's own markup; that whitespace has been normalized to a single space here and was verified against leginfo's raw HTML directly. This clause does not address what makes collective-bargaining-agreement language "expressly address[]" digital replica uses, nor does it identify which unions' agreements currently contain such language, neither of which was researched for this document. No case law construing either safe harbor has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

WHAT UNENFORCEABILITY DOES NOT REACH: THE REST OF THE CONTRACT, AND ANY EXCLUSIVITY GRANTS, ARE UNAFFECTED
Subdivision (b) narrows what a finding of unenforceability under subdivision (a) actually does. It states that "this section does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a)" — so even where a specific digital-replica provision is unenforceable, the rest of Taylor Morgan's and Acme Studios LLC's contract is not automatically affected by that one provision's unenforceability. The same subdivision separately preserves exclusivity grants: the statute "does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a)." An exclusivity grant tied to a digital-replica provision therefore is not itself unwound merely because the digital-replica provision it relates to becomes unenforceable under subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a) and does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — limited effect of unenforceability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of subdivision (b)'s own limiting language — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how a specific contract's severability clause, if any, would interact with subdivision (b), or about what counts as an "exclusivity grant... related to" a digital-replica provision in a specific contract, neither of which this document evaluates. This clause quotes subdivision (b) in full as one integrated sentence pair from the same statutory subsection; it is one source, not two independent ones. No case law construing subdivision (b), including how courts have treated the exclusivity-grant carve-out, has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF 'DIGITAL REPLICA'
Section 927(c)(1) defines "digital replica," for purposes of this section, as "a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation that is readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual that is embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission in which the actual individual either did not actually perform or appear, or the actual individual did perform or appear, but the fundamental character of the performance or appearance has been materially altered." This definition reaches two distinct situations: a representation of an individual who never actually performed or appeared in the underlying recording or work at all, and a representation of an individual who did perform or appear, but whose actual performance or appearance was materially altered such that its fundamental character changed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation that is readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual that is embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission in which the actual individual either did not actually perform or appear, or the actual individual did perform or appear, but the fundamental character of the performance or appearance has been materially altered."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — statutory definition of "digital replica" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(c)(1)'s own definition — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific representation of a particular individual does or does not meet this definition, which depends on the specific representation and is not evaluated here. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(c)(1); it does not compare this definition against the separately defined "digital replica" term used in Civil Code section 3344.1(a)(2)(B)(ii)(I) (already quoted and sourced elsewhere in this corpus's Right of Publicity Demand Letter Information Sheet) beyond noting, in this document's scope clause, that the two statutes serve different purposes; a side-by-side textual comparison of the two definitions was not performed for this document. No case law construing this definition has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

WHAT 'DIGITAL REPLICA' DOES NOT INCLUDE: AUTHORIZED SAMPLING, REMIXING, AND REMASTERING
Section 927(c)(2) narrows the definition described in the preceding clause by excluding certain ordinary audio and audiovisual production practices, so long as they are authorized by the copyright holder: "'Digital replica' does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyrightholder." A copyright-holder-authorized sample, remix, master, or remaster of an existing sound recording or audiovisual work therefore falls outside this section's "digital replica" definition on the statute's own terms, regardless of whether it otherwise resembles the kind of computer-generated representation described in subdivision (c)(1).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Digital replica” does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyrightholder."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 927(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — exclusion for authorized sampling, remixing, and remastering (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=927.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(c)(2)'s own exclusion language — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific sample, remix, master, or remaster is or is not authorized by a copyright holder in a specific case, which is a separate factual and copyright-law question this document does not evaluate. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(c)(2), which itself does not define "authorized" or identify who must grant that authorization when more than one copyright holder has an interest in the underlying work; this document does not research or resolve that question, and does not address federal copyright law's own separate rules on joint authorship or licensing that might bear on it. No case law construing this exclusion has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

DIGITAL REPLICA CONTRACT PROVISION — DOCUMENTATION RECORD
This record documents information about a digital-replica provision in a personal or professional services agreement, for reference against Labor Code section 927's statutory conditions described in this information sheet. It does not itself determine whether the provision described is enforceable or unenforceable under that statute.

Individual: Taylor Morgan
Other contracting party: Acme Studios LLC
Date the agreement was signed: September 1, 2026

Description of the intended uses of the digital replica stated in the provision, if any: Use of a synthetic voice model in dubbed foreign-language versions of the same film

Was the individual represented, in connection with this provision, by legal counsel who negotiated the digital replica rights on the individual's behalf, by a labor union whose collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses digital replica uses, by both, or by neither: Represented by personal entertainment counsel who negotiated the digital replica license terms

This record does not itself constitute the contract, does not modify the underlying agreement between Taylor Morgan and Acme Studios LLC, and does not resolve whether the described provision meets, or fails to meet, any specific condition of Labor Code section 927(a).

CLOSING STATEMENT AND SIGNATURE
This information sheet describes California Labor Code section 927 as of September 1, 2026 and does not describe any other jurisdiction's law on digital replicas, personal-services contracts, or performer representation. It is not legal advice, does not evaluate any specific contract provision between Taylor Morgan and Acme Studios LLC, and does not determine whether any specific provision is enforceable or unenforceable under section 927 or any other law.

expectedJSON.body: Section 927(c)(1) defines "digital replica," for purposes of this section, as "a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation that is readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual that is embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission in which the actual individual either did not actually perform or appear, or the actual individual did perform or appear, but the fundamental character of the performance or appearance has been materially altered." This definition reaches two distinct situations: a representation of an individual who never actually performed or appeared in the underlying recording or work at all, and a representation of an individual who did perform or appear, but whose actual performance or appearance was materially altered such that its fundamental character changed.
